standard.title: Networks and data transmission
standard.description: Examine how digital systems form networks to transmit data
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explore the transmission of different types of data between digital systems (AC9TDI4K02). They understand that data can move between devices. They have not yet examined how networks are structured, how devices connect to form them, or how data is structured for transmission (packets).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students examine how digital systems connect in different ways to form networks, and explain how data is structured and transmitted through a network from source to destination.

nodes.label: How separate systems connect to form networks
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how separate digital systems can be connected in different ways to exchange data
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two ways a device can connect to a network (e.g. cable, Wi-Fi) and explain that connecting devices allows them to exchange data
nodes.typical_width: Explain how a laptop or device can connect to a network via a physical cable or radio waves (Wi-Fi/Bluetooth); compare when each type of connection is more appropriate
wider: Investigate how satellite phones provide network access where mobile phone networks are unavailable, such as in remote Arnhem Land communities — explaining why different network infrastructure is needed in these locations
Compare how the same device (e.g. a laptop) uses different connection types in different situations — wired at school, Wi-Fi at home, mobile data travelling — and why the network experience differs

response_modes.reason: Students commonly confuse the connection type (cable vs wireless) with the network itself — thinking the wire is the internet rather than a path to it. Multiple connection contexts (home, school, remote area) help students see that the network is the shared infrastructure, not the physical medium.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The satellite/remote community direction is rich — it makes network infrastructure visible as a designed, imperfect system rather than a background convenience, and raises equity questions about unequal access that are substantive and age-appropriate.
success_criteria: Names at least two ways a device can connect to a network
Explains that connecting devices allows data to be exchanged between them
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have not grasped that separate devices connect to form networks cannot follow the packet transmission model in N2 — the path a packet travels requires understanding there is a network of connected devices for it to traverse.

nodes.label: How data travels through a network
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how data is structured into packets and transmitted through multiple devices from source to destination
nodes.minimum_width: Explain that data is broken into packets for transmission and these packets travel from the source through multiple devices to the destination
nodes.typical_width: Describe how data is broken into packets, transmitted through multiple intermediate devices, and reassembled at the destination; explain why breaking data into packets is useful (e.g. packets can take different routes, errors affect only one packet)
wider: Investigate what happens when a packet is lost or delayed — how does the destination device detect missing data and request retransmission?
Compare how packet size and number of intermediate devices (hops) affects transmission speed and reliability in different network types

response_modes.reason: The packet model is counter-intuitive — students expect data to travel as a single stream like water through a pipe. Tracing a message as packets through a diagrammed network (source → router → router → destination) makes the multi-step transmission legible and challenges the 'direct connection' mental model.

success_criteria: Explains that data is broken into packets for network transmission
Describes that packets travel through multiple devices to reach the destination
